title: Air potato, rosary pea, umbrella tree: how to spot them in your Sebastian yard, and the Nov. 14 Weed Wrangle
seoTitle: Sebastian Invasive Plants: Air Potato, Rosary Pea & More
description: How to spot air potato, rosary pea and umbrella tree in your Sebastian yard, how to remove them safely, and how to join the city's Nov. 14 Weed Wrangle.
dek: The City of Sebastian is inviting neighbors to pull three invasive plants out of Stormwater Park next Saturday. The same three may be growing along your fence line right now. Here is how to recognize them, what to do about them, and how to sign up.
facebook: Ever seen a vine with "potatoes" hanging off it, or bright red seeds with a black dot, in your Sebastian yard? Those are invasive plants, and one of them is poisonous. Here's how to spot three of them, and how to join the city's Weed Wrangle on Nov. 14.

how to get rid of air potato

body.text: Walk the back edge of almost any Sebastian lot and you may find a plant that does not belong there. Some climb the fence. Some sneak up into the oak. One of them has seeds pretty enough to string into a bracelet, and poisonous enough that you should never do it.

On Nov. 5, the City of Sebastian invited residents to an Invasive Species Weed Wrangle. Volunteers will pull three plants out of Sebastian Stormwater Park: air potato vine, Australian umbrella tree and rosary pea. The city says these plants crowd out native vegetation, reduce biodiversity and degrade habitat. Removing them is meant to help native plants come back.

body.title: The short version
body.text: Weed Wrangle: Saturday, Nov. 14, 9 to 11 a.m., Sebastian Stormwater Park, 297 Englar Drive. Sign up on the city's online form (the link is on the event page at cityofsebastian.org). At home: learn the three plants below, never move air potato bulbils to a new spot, and keep children and pets away from rosary pea seeds.
Air potato: the vine that grows "potatoes" in the air

Air potato is a vine that twines up anything it can reach, often all the way into tree canopies. UF/IFAS says its stems can reach 60 feet. The leaves are heart-shaped and can grow up to about 8 inches long.

The giveaway is the bulbils. These are round, light brown, potato-looking lumps that grow where the leaves meet the stem. UF/IFAS says they range from pea-size to about five inches across, and one plant can make hundreds. Each bulbil can start a new plant. The vine also grows from tubers just under the soil.

Air potato is on Florida's noxious weed list, and UF/IFAS rates it "Prohibited." Do not confuse it with native greenbrier (Smilax), which can look similar at a glance. UF/IFAS notes that air potato has more main veins in each leaf.

items: Cut the vines back before new bulbils form, which UF/IFAS says is typically late summer.
Pick up bulbils in winter, when the leaves die back and they are easier to see.
Dig out the tubers in the top few inches of soil.
Do not toss bulbils into the woods or a neighbor's lot. UF/IFAS lists freezing, or yard waste or landfill disposal where your local service accepts them.
Plan to keep at it. UF/IFAS says it can take repeated yearly work over four to five years to clear a spot completely.

body.text: Rosary pea: pretty seeds, serious poison

Rosary pea is the one to take most seriously, especially if you have kids, grandkids or pets. It is a vine that turns woody at the base and grows a deep taproot. The leaves are made of many small leaflets, and the flowers look like small, light pink pea blossoms, mostly in late summer and fall.

The seeds are what you will notice. The pods are about 3 to 4 centimeters long, roughly an inch and a half. When they dry and twist open, they show three to eight shiny, bright red seeds, each with a black spot at one end. UF/IFAS says the seeds contain abrin, a toxin, and that crushing and eating the seeds is dangerous to people and livestock.

Like air potato, rosary pea is on Florida's noxious weed list and rated "Prohibited" by UF/IFAS. Birds carry the seeds long distances, and seeds can sit in the soil for a long time, so new plants keep popping up.

items: Pull young seedlings by hand. Wear gloves.
Pick off the pods and seeds before they open and drop. Bag them and keep them away from children and pets.
Mature plants are hard to pull because of the taproot. UF/IFAS suggests asking your local UF/IFAS Extension office or a licensed professional before using any herbicide.
Check the same spot again in a few months. The seeds left in the soil will sprout.

body.text: Australian umbrella tree: the houseplant that got too big

Many Florida homeowners planted this one on purpose. Australian umbrella tree, also called octopus tree or Schefflera actinophylla, was sold for years as a small landscape or indoor plant. It can grow to about 40 feet. The leaves look like an umbrella, with 7 to 16 long leaflets fanning out from one stem. In summer and early fall it puts out large red flower clusters at the tips of the stems, followed by small, round, dark purple fruit.

The UF/IFAS Assessment of Non-Native Plants lists it as "Invasive (No Uses)" for central and south Florida, and Indian River County is on its list of counties where it is found. A UF/IFAS Extension article says birds spread the seeds, and small plants that homeowners set out have grown into large trees that took over their yards.

Do not mix it up with dwarf schefflera (Schefflera arboricola). That is a rounded shrub, seldom taller than 10 feet, and it is on the Florida-Friendly Landscaping list. The big umbrella tree is the problem.

items: Walk your yard this weekend. Look along fences, in hedges and up into trees for heart-shaped vine leaves, brown bulbils, red-and-black seeds, or a tall tree with umbrella-shaped leaves.
If you find rosary pea, deal with the seeds first. Gloves on, pods off, bagged, and out of reach of kids and pets.
Pull or cut what you safely can. Keep air potato bulbils and tubers from landing anywhere new.
For a big umbrella tree or a mature vine you cannot pull, call your local UF/IFAS Extension office or a licensed professional for advice before you spray anything. Always follow the product label.

Join the Weed Wrangle on Saturday, Nov. 14, from 9 to 11 a.m. at Sebastian Stormwater Park, 297 Englar Drive. Register through the online form on the city's event page. It is a good way to learn the plants with your own eyes.

body.text: One more tip: a plant you remove is only half the job. Once a spot is clear, check it again in a month or two, because these three are good at coming back.

faq.q: When is the Sebastian Weed Wrangle?
faq.a: Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, from 9 to 11 a.m. at Sebastian Stormwater Park, 297 Englar Drive. Volunteers sign up through an online form linked on the City of Sebastian's event page.

faq.q: How do I identify air potato vine?
faq.a: Look for a climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves and round, light brown, potato-like bulbils growing where the leaves meet the stem. UF/IFAS says the bulbils range from pea-size to about five inches across.
Yes. UF/IFAS says the shiny red seeds with a black spot contain abrin, and crushing and eating them is dangerous to people and livestock. Keep children and pets away from the seeds.

faq.q: Is the umbrella tree invasive in Florida?
faq.a: Yes. The UF/IFAS Assessment of Non-Native Plants lists Australian umbrella tree (Schefflera actinophylla) as Invasive (No Uses) in central and south Florida. Dwarf schefflera is a different plant and is not on that list.

faq.q: How do I get rid of air potato for good?
faq.a: Cut vines before bulbils form, collect bulbils in winter, dig out tubers, and do not move bulbils to new spots. UF/IFAS says it can take yearly work over four to five years to clear an area completely.
